planting.note: Plant cloves in fall about 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes so roots establish before winter; in mild-winter regions it can also go in as a late-winter planting for an earlier, smaller harvest.

directions: Thermidrome is a softneck garlic that traces to the Drome valley of southeastern France, long favored there for its earliness and reliability in a maritime climate. Plant individual cloves pointed end up about 2 inches deep, mulch over winter, and keep beds weeded through spring since garlic competes poorly with weeds. Because it matures earlier and stores well into the following year, it is a dependable choice for gardeners in milder, wetter winter regions where hardneck types can rot. The flavor is notably milder than most hardnecks, making it popular for raw use.

planting.note: Plant cloves 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes so roots establish before winter dormancy; mulch heavily in colder zones.

directions: Asian Tempest is an Asiatic-type hardneck garlic that came to American growers through an Oregon gardener who obtained it from South Korea, and it has since become known for its vigorous growth and heavy bulbil production on the scape. Cloves are fewer but plump, and the flavor starts mellow when cooked but turns notably sharp and intense when eaten raw. Grow it like other hardnecks, removing the curling scape in late spring to redirect energy into bulb size, and harvest once the lower leaves begin to brown. It stores only moderately well compared to Porcelain types, so plan to use it earlier in the season.

planting.note: Plant cloves in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; a mid-season hardneck that does well across a broad range of climates including the Midwest.

directions: Vietnamese Red is a purple-striped hardneck garlic prized for a creamy, buttery texture and a sweetness that intensifies with roasting, distinguishing it from sharper rocambole types. Bulbs typically hold 9 to 12 large cloves wrapped in skins streaked with rose and purple. Grow it as a standard hardneck: plant cloves pointed end up in fall, cut the scape once it curls to push more energy into the bulb, and cure the harvested bulbs in a shaded, airy spot for a few weeks before storage. It has become a favorite among cooks who want sweetness without excessive heat.

planting.note: Plant cloves in fall; Turban types like Uzbek sprout and mature earliest of all garlic groups, so they can also be planted a bit later than other hardnecks in mild climates.

directions: Uzbek is a Turban-group hardneck garlic traced to Uzbekistan and brought into North American seed stock decades ago; Turban types are named for the way their bulb wrappers twist and swirl like fabric wound around the cloves. It is among the earliest garlics to mature, with shiny purple-streaked skins over big, earthy-flavored cloves that carry a surprising spicy kick. Because Turban types generally store more briefly than Porcelain or Silverskin garlic, plan to use Uzbek bulbs within a few months of curing rather than holding them for a full year. Give it the same fall planting, spring scape removal, and full-sun culture as other hardnecks.

planting.note: Plant cloves in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; this is one of the earliest hardnecks to mature, so watch for yellowing lower leaves ahead of other varieties.

directions: Chinese Pink is a Porcelain-type hardneck known for finishing about two weeks ahead of most other hardneck garlics, making it useful for gardeners wanting an early harvest or a hedge against unpredictable weather. Bulbs are smaller, typically holding just 4 to 6 plump cloves wrapped in blush pink-tinged wrappers, with a flavor many describe as gentler and easier on the stomach than sharper varieties. Grow and cure it like other hardnecks: plant in fall, remove the scape once it curls, and harvest when the lower leaves begin to brown. Its mild character makes it a good entry point for cooks who find stronger hardneck garlics overpowering raw.

scientific_name: Allium cepa var. aggregatum 'Yellow Potato Onion'

planting.note: Plant small bulbs in fall for the largest harvest the following summer in mild-winter regions, or in very early spring as soon as soil is workable where winters are severe.

directions: Yellow Potato Onion is a true heirloom multiplier onion documented in American gardens since before 1790, grown from small saved bulbs rather than seed. Each planted bulb divides underground into a cluster of new bulbs ranging from an inch to several inches across, so a gardener can keep a perpetual supply going year after year without buying sets or seed again. It tolerates drought better than seed-grown onions and is widely adapted across the country, with fall planting generally producing larger bulbs than spring planting. Set bulbs about 2 inches deep with the tip just at the soil surface, and harvest once the tops die back, saving the largest bulbs to replant and the rest for the kitchen.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall, 4-6 inches deep, in gritty, well-drained soil; like most ornamental alliums it dislikes wet winter soil and rots if drainage is poor.

directions: Red Mohican is a selection of Allium amethystinum, a drumstick-type ornamental onion native to the eastern Mediterranean, distinguished from other drumstick alliums by its deep wine-red flower heads topped with a shaggy, crest-like tuft of buds that open into small white florets. It blooms on tall, sturdy stems in late spring to early summer, well after the earlier globe-type alliums have finished, extending the ornamental allium season in a border or cutting garden. Once established it is quite drought tolerant and needs little supplemental water, and its flowers are a strong draw for bees and other pollinators. Leave the strappy foliage to die back naturally after bloom so the bulb can recharge for the following year.
